extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students / beginning proof writers
extracted.subtask_description: Guide to techniques, conventions, and heuristics for writing clear, correct mathematical proofs, covering direct proofs, contrapositives, contradiction, iff proofs, induction, and presentation/ drafting practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: proof as logical explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: A “proof” of the theorem is a logical explanation of why the theorem is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proof must explain WHY the claimed statement holds — not just assert it. The explanation should be logical and connect assumptions to conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct proof: assume hypothesis and derive conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: A direct proof: start by assuming that statement A is true (write that down as the first step) and proceed logically, one step at a time, building on this information until you have shown that statement B is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try a direct proof first as a rule of thumb. Explicitly state the assumption (the hypothesis) and use only valid logical steps to reach the conclusion. If A is false then the implication is vacuously true, so the natural place to begin is to assume A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write proofs in clear, complete English sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: An important point is that a proof is always written in English! There are mathematical symbols mixed in with the words, but you must write clear, complete, English sentences, one after another until you’ve made your way through to statement B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use full sentences to explain each logical step; include mathematical notation only where it supplements the prose. The goal is communication to the reader; clarity and completeness matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use an end-of-proof symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: Finally, write an “end-of-proof” symbol like Q.E.D. or □ to show that you’ve finished the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a conventional end marker so the reader knows the argument is complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting process: three-sheet workflow
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of the time, it takes THREE sheets of paper to write a proof: (1) scratch paper for trying ideas, (2) a first attempt where you try to write the proof neatly but may discover errors, and (3) a final neat sheet with the polished proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect to do scratchwork and revisions; present only the polished final version to the reader. The final write-up should be clear, complete, and communicative — not the messy scratchwork.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrapositive proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The contrapositive of 'If A then B' is 'If not B then not A' and is logically the same statement. To prove the original theorem you can start by assuming statement B is false, then show statement A is false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a contrapositive proof when it appears easier to deduce not A from not B than to deduce B from A. The contrapositive is an equivalent formulation, so proving it suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove 'If A then B' by contradiction, assume A is true and also assume B is false, then build on these assumptions until you obtain a contradiction, showing that the assumption 'B is false' is impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the argument so the contradictory statement is explicitly identified. Contradiction proofs can also prove standalone existence/nonexistence statements (e.g., Euclid's proof that primes are infinite) by assuming the negation and deriving an impossibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful interpretation of what a proof claims (avoid overreading)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful about what a proof actually says; conditional statements proved under an assumption that turned out false do not necessarily imply concrete constructive claims outside that assumption (example: Euclid's proof shows that IF only finitely many primes existed then a certain construction would be prime; but since the premise is false, the construction need not always produce a prime).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always check the hypothesis under which the proof operates and avoid inferring stronger/unwarranted conclusions from the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: If and only if (bi-directional) proofs requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: For a statement 'A if and only if B' you must prove two implications: 'If A then B' AND 'If B then A'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write two separate proofs (one for each direction). You can use different proof methods for each direction (direct, contrapositive, etc.). If you only write one direction, you have not proved the equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set equality via two inclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: To show X = Y for sets, first show 'if x ∈ X then x ∈ Y' (X ⊂ Y), then show 'if y ∈ Y then y ∈ X' (Y ⊂ X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proving both inclusions establishes equality; state each inclusion as its own implication and prove it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by induction: base case and inductive step
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove statements A_n for n = 1, 2, 3, ... by induction: Step 1 — show A_1 is true (base case). Step 2 — prove that IF A_n is true then A_{n+1} is true (inductive step).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why these two steps suffice (recursion): the base case starts the chain, and the inductive step propagates truth to all integers. Use induction when statements are indexed by integers and you can derive n+1 from n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use heuristics: try direct proof first, then contrapositive or contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: It may not be obvious which variety of proof to use, but a good rule of thumb is to try a direct proof first. If you don’t see how, try proving the contrapositive; if that fails, consider contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are practical heuristics for selecting a proof technique; experiment using scratchwork to see which approach yields a workable chain of reasoning.
